students through the education system.

Developing a Successful Growth Model

In the states demonstrating success in implementing student growth
models, one commonality stands out: Commitment to the growth
model by three key groups:
Directors of Measurement/Assessment.
Directors of Accountability.
Directors of Information-Technology.
Measurement/Assessment specialists understand the state
assessments and will need to be able to understand and explain
growth data derived from those assessments.
Accountability directors will be involved in the use of these data,
particularly as they pertain to accountability initiatives.
CIOs/IT directors will often be tasked will helping to disseminate the
results of the growth model.
These directors become mavens for the work to others within their
organization that reach out to the diverse range of stakeholders.

Describing Student Growth

Measuring student growth, even with a vertical scale, is not a simple
task.
Some believe a vertical scale simplifies the task of measuring
student growth.
Even with an interval (or ratio) scale, growth is not easy to interpret.
Consider, for example, height.
A child might grow 4 inches between ages 3 and 4.
4 inches is a well understood quantity.
The 4 inch increase becomes really meaningful only when understood
alongside the growth of other 3 to 4 year olds.
Student growth percentiles were developed to provide a normative
context for describing student growth.

Student Growth Percentiles

Should we be surprised with a child’s current achievement given their
prior achievement?
Student growth percentiles answer this question.
Consider a low achieving student with 75th percentile growth and a
high achieving student with 25th percentile growth.
The low achieving student grew at a rate exceeding 75 percent of their
academic peers.
The high achieving student grew at a rate exceeding just 25 percent of
their academic peers.
The low achiever’s growth is more exemplary (probabilistically) than
the high achiever’s.
Judgments about the adequacy of student growth require external
criteria.

What are the relevant questions for parents?

Different stakeholder groups will have different questions [Yen, 2007].

Parent Questions
Did my child make a year’s worth of progress in a year?
Is my child making sufficient growth toward meeting state
standards?
Is my child growing at the same rate in Math and Reading or is
she/he experiencing lower or higher growth in one content area
compared to the other?
Did my child grow as much this year as last year?

What are the relevant questions for teachers?
Different stakeholder groups will have different questions [Yen, 2007].

Teacher Questions
Did my students make a year’s worth of progress in a year?
Did my students make sufficient growth toward meeting state
standards?
Did my students make as much progress as students in other
classrooms within my school or across schools within the
complex area and state?
Did my students learn as much in mathematics as they did in
reading?
Are there students with unusually low growth who need special
attention?
Do these growth results generally appear consistent with or
differ from what I already know about how my students have
progressed during the school year?

Do students in certain demographic subgroups show as much
growth as other demographic subgroups?
Are our students growing consistently over multiple years?

Going from Students to Classrooms/Schools

It’s of interest to examine schools, classrooms and programs where
students demonstrate, on average, extraordinarily high and low
student growth.
To summarize the student growth percentiles associated with a
school (or other grouping) calculate the median of the student
growth percentiles.
If students were randomly assigned to the group, expect to see a
median of 50.
Values greatly above or below 50 are of interest in identifying best
practices or providing extra support.
Examining growth with achievement sheds new light on school
performance.
